extracted.intended_audience: editors, publishers, and editorial staff of peer-reviewed biomedical/medical journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, implementing, and enforcing conflict-of-interest (COI) policies for peer-reviewed medical journals, covering definition, disclosure, management, and oversight for authors, reviewers, and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear definition the journal uses as to what is conflict of interest and who is captured in the definition. Sample definition: Conflict of interest exists when a participant in the publication process (author, peer reviewer or editor) has a competing interest that could unduly influence (or be reasonably seen to do so) his or her responsibilities in the publication process (submission of manuscripts, peer review, editorial decisions and communication between authors, reviewers and editors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should explicitly state who is covered (authors, peer reviewers, editors) and which stages of the process are implicated (submission, review, editorial decisions, communications). The definition should include the 'reasonable observer' standard: whether a reasonable observer might wonder if behavior/judgment was motivated by competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Competing Interests (broadened beyond financial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement of examples of the types of competing interests (and their definitions) the journal says must be declared. Should include the following as examples but there could be others: Financial ties; Academic commitments; Personal relationships; Political or religious beliefs; Institutional affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WAME recommends moving beyond just financial conflicts to include: effects of clinical income (e.g., physicians' income from procedures), 'intellectual passion' (scholarly commitment), personal relationships (friends/colleagues/competitors), political or religious beliefs, and institutional affiliations. Journals should articulate examples and definitions that fit their context and recognize that multiple competing interests can coexist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring Conflicts of Interest (what/when/how to disclose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear statements on (a) what is to be declared, when and to whom; (b) format for declaration; (c) a journal’s role in asking additional questions or seeking clarification about disclosures and (d) consequences for failing to disclose before or after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals rely on declarers because routine monitoring is not possible; therefore questionnaires/forms should be designed to maximize likelihood of reporting relevant COIs. Specify timing (submission, revision, pre-publication, post-publication updates), required format (written forms, standardized templates), the recipient of disclosures (editorial office), and follow-up procedures when disclosures are incomplete or ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing Conflicts of Interest (policy on actions and publication of disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement on how conflict of interest will be managed by the journal, including the position that all relevant conflict of interest disclosures (or the declaration of no conflict of interest) will be published with the article and clarity about what conflict of interest situations will result in a manuscript not being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should describe the range of management options (e.g., publishing disclosures, excluding conflicted reviewers or editors, rejecting manuscripts when COI is sufficiently impairing) and make clear which situations lead to exclusion from consideration. Journals use various rules and these must be communicated to all participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full Written Disclosure as the Foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: The backbone of managing conflicts of interest is full written disclosure; without it, nothing else is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that disclosure is necessary though imperfect. Because journals cannot routinely monitor or investigate all potential COIs, comprehensive self-disclosure is required from participants. Journals should publish disclosures with articles to enable transparency for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal-Specific Standards and Editorial Judgment (no universal threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: WAME did not prescribe a universal standard for when meaningful conflict of interest exists. Rather, it defined and recommended elements of COI policies and encouraged journals to establish their own standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should set operational definitions and standards appropriate to their context, discipline, and culture. Editors must exercise judgment about the strength of a conflict and its potential to impair objectivity; WAME offers factors to consider but leaves specific thresholds to individual journals to avoid global one-size-fits-all rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigating and Acting on Failures to Disclose
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have a responsibility for investigating, and if relevant acting, if competing interests surface after a manuscript is submitted or published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations of failure to declare COI must be taken seriously. Policies should specify investigation procedures, possible corrective actions (e.g., corrections, expressions of concern, retractions), and sanctions for deliberate nondisclosure. Journals should transparently report outcomes of such investigations when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply COI Policies to All Participants (authors, peer reviewers, editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement addresses conflicts of interests threatening all participants in the research and publication continuum, including authors, peer reviewers and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies must cover reviewers and editors as well as authors. Particular attention should be given to editor-owner relationships (addressed in a separate WAME policy) because these can affect accuracy and credibility. Journals should define expectations and management steps for each role (e.g., recusal, exclusion from decision-making).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and Accessibility of COI Policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should make COI policies readily accessible to everyone and publish with every article all relevant author disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should be publicly available (website, author instructions) and disclosures should be visible in published articles so readers can assess potential influences. Accessibility also aids compliance and public trust.
